Pretty good, but the endgame is where it falls short.
So what can I say about Fallout 76? Honestly, it’s pretty good, but it definitely has its flaws.
The biggest issue for me is the endgame. Once you’ve completed the main missions, side missions, events, endgame bosses, raids, and most of the major content, there isn’t really much left that feels worth playing toward. At that point, you’re mostly just leveling up, collecting resources, improving your gear, and repeating the same activities.
Now, some people genuinely love that kind of gameplay loop, and if that’s you, more power to you. There’s definitely a lot to enjoy in Fallout 76 if you like constantly grinding, building your character, collecting items, and improving your camp.
But as a Fallout fan, eventually you reach a point where you’ve experienced most of what the game has to offer, and there isn’t much left that gives you that feeling of, “I want to keep playing because I have something new to accomplish.”
I still think Fallout 76 is a good game, especially compared to where it was at launch, and there’s plenty of fun to be had. I just wish the endgame had more meaningful progression and more reasons to keep coming back after you’ve completed the majority of the content.
Overall: Good game, great Fallout world, but the endgame needs more to keep veteran players engaged.

430 hours in and I think I have a good grasp at most things in the game. I purposely avoided the game at its original release because of the bad reviews and also I was not interested in a multi-player fallout game. But saw it was on sale for really cheap and figured why not, I'll give it a shot all these years later. And overall it's pretty solid.

I had a lot of difficulty starting the game on my PC, I had stutter problems with my 4070ti super card and had AI work me through file edits and nvidia settings to fix the issue. Once that was done, then the next problem happened... the bombardment of missions. I didn't know what quest was what, controls were weird, and didn't even know how to use VATS until several days into the game. The learning curve for me was pretty high despite having played several fallout games in the past. I also never played multi-player before much so I was really confused about the environment -- basically how players interact with each other when exploring or during quests, or even how teams worked, just overall game mechanics was weird for me. And every time I thought I understood how the currency system works, I'm tossed a new currency unit to figure out and how to use it. I basically just roamed around and tried to explore parts of the map without dying.

But once you get to level 50 then some of those higher level weapons and armor you can use. And getting power armor helped with carry limits and staying alive.

But then the next major thing happened and it's the stashbox limits. You can put 1200 weight units into the box and once that fills up, the game becomes inventory management simulator. So the remedy is to shell out $15/mo or whatever it is for Fallout 1st so you can store unlimited scrap in a scrapbox.... but mind you the stashbox still has the 1200 limit as before but the catch is all your scrap should be removed to leave more room for weapons and armor.

So once I hit around level 200 I caved and got Fallout 1st and it's made the game much more enjoyable, unfortunately at an added cost. I'm now level 430-ish and decently strong, but I still have a ways to go.

Now for the game itself...
Some quests are decent, some are boring, some mediocre, and some genuinely fun or interesting.
Sound effects are pretty cool, like the gatling gun is pretty awesome for the first time.
Voice acting is hilarious at times which actually makes me chuckle.
The area to explore is pretty large and diverse.
Enemies are pretty cool overall and a wide variety.
I'm maxing out the game basically and the visuals are nice for an older game, but would love to see what they can do with the next Fallout game.
Controls took me a long time to figure out, but that's me with every game basically.
The other players in the game are great... I've encountered I think zero issues in 8 months of playing.
Some of the lore and game features like "infestations" make no logical sense, the devs just make new ways to fight enemies but it's all the same thing under the hood. 

If you can get this for really cheap, like 5 bucks or less, it's a great way to test out the game and see if you like it. It's one of those games that I thought I wouldn't like, but here I am 8 months later still playing and paying my monthly dues to Todd.

At its core, Fallout 76 offers a genuinely engaging world. Its atmospheric Appalachian map, rich lore, and welcoming community make it a game worth loving. However, it is fundamentally held back by an outdated Creation Engine and poor management that fail to meet modern expectations.

> Brutal Performance on Modern Hardware: Even with high-end, performant modern PC hardware, the game remains a struggle to run smoothly—frequently choking during crowded events due to engine caps, CPU bottlenecks, and outdated optimization.

> Archaic Engine Friction: Severe frame drops, high-refresh-rate physics bugs, and input lag turn basic movement and combat into a chore.

> Persistent Glitches: Unresponsive hit registration, freeze-prone sign-in screens, broken UI elements, and clunky C.A.M.P. building mechanics constantly disrupt immersion.

> Exploits & Bots: Seeing accounts with absurd levels exceeding 32,000 highlights unchecked XP exploits and poor server oversight.

> Outdated Quality-of-Life: Frequent server desync, inventory limits tailored to sell subscriptions, and stealth updates erode player trust.

Beneath the technical wreckage lies a beautiful game, but its engine bugs and clunky design drive players away far too early.

1,169 hours in, so I think I’ve earned the right to say this: Fallout 76 is both much better than its reputation and exactly as janky as people say it is.**

The game has come an absurdly long way from launch. Appalachia is genuinely fun to explore, the CAMP system can consume entire evenings by itself, public events are great when the server is active, and the amount of build tinkering available once you get into weapons, armor, perks, legendary effects, mutations, and endgame gear is ridiculous.

There is always something else to chase. A better legendary roll. Another plan. Another piece of armor. Another build idea. Another event. Another completely unnecessary CAMP renovation because apparently the staircase being three feet to the left was unacceptable.

That said, this is still Bethesda.

Bugs range from funny to infuriating. Balance changes sometimes seem completely disconnected from how people actually play. Certain grinds feel deliberately stretched out, currencies are capped for reasons known only to Todd Howard, and the game occasionally decides that something which worked perfectly yesterday simply does not work today.

The endgame is also less about “beating” Fallout 76 and more about developing increasingly specific personal objectives until you realize you’ve spent several hours optimizing a weapon that was already killing everything perfectly fine.

And yet...

**I have 1,169 hours.**

That probably says more than anything else I could write.

Fallout 76 is messy, grindy, occasionally broken, sometimes baffling, and one of the games I keep coming back to anyway. If you enjoy Fallout, exploration, character builds, collecting gear, base building, and the kind of multiplayer where you can spend an evening fighting giant monsters with strangers before going home to rearrange furniture, there is an enormous amount of game here.

Would I recommend it?

After 1,169 hours, saying no would be a little dishonest.

So. This one is complicated... I am a big Fallout fan and when 76 got announced I was so hyped! I knew that I would play it mostly solo but that didnt bother me because I did the same with ESO. So I preordered it, downloaded it on the bethesda launcher (where you had to play it back then) and started it.

And? I enjoyed it! ...Mostly. It played exactly like Fallout 4 (Which ist important to remember) and had a cool world with a lot of fun things to do. But I also had a big feeling of kenopsia. (A uncanny valley like experience when youre in an empty place that feels like it should be populated)

That feeling was because back then the only humans in the game were supposed to be other players, but the servers could only hold 24 people in one map. THATS NOT ENOUGH FOR A MAP THIS BIG!!! I still enjoyed it for quite some time, got into building and exploring and had my fun. 

But the absence of NPCs had 2 big problems: First a lack of negaging quests and story and second what made Fallout feel so good in the first place! Fallout was always the post apocalyptic world, where humans try to regain control of the world and succeed. Going to places like Diamond City was so cool because of this feeling. Not here. It felt like humans lost.

But how is it now? I described this to tell what many people think FO76 still is despite this being its first few seasons. Now it got many NPCs, great places to explore and an amazing big Fallout world. Now it IS like FO4. Just bigger. And while I would still say, that it really hurts the game that the map is so big because we still dont have enough NPCs and only 24 other players on a server is way too few. A server could easily hold 128 People in my opinion. But all in all: I like the game. And if you enjoyed FO3 or 4 then I would highly recommend you to try it!

Feels like an MMO, and operates well with controller.  There are a lot of quests to do if you want to get "caught up" with everyone else.  But I suggest taking your time with it, and explore the various character build options.  Many builds will work best in certain situations, so you will find yourself switching perk cards around when changing activities.  Enjoy the stories that are here... you have a lot of content to get through that wasn't here when the game released.

Controller support could be better with some dead zone options.  Would also be better to have sliders for look sensitivity, ADS sensitivity, and cursor sensitivity... instead we have one sensitivity slider that controls all three.  You can edit the ini files to adjust some of these, but shouldn't have to do that to get basic sensitivity adjusted properly.

The end game seems to be centered around base building and finishing your collections of various things like magazines, bobbleheads, and plans/recipes.  Not everyone is into that sort of thing, which is why I say take your time with the quests.  I've put in a good bit of time with the game, so I can tell you that it is not a game for everyone, but it is a decent game.

I'm not a big fan of having stash space tied to a subscription, but you do have enough stash space without Fallout 1st that you can store what you need for your building and crafting needs... it just might take a bit longer to complete bigger building projects.

Don't go into this game expecting something like all of the other Fallout games.  It is not a sequel, and does not play like previous games.  A perfect example of this is the public events.  You might have a great sneak build that you use for exploration and questing, but it becomes useless as soon as you enter a public event.  Now you need to tag multiple enemies quickly before they die, so that you get the experience from the kills.  Not every build will hold up in this environment, and such events feel nothing like FO3 or 4.

I like the game overall, but also recognize that you need to manage your expectations going into it.

I've played this game for what I consider to be an ungodly amount of hours for what it deserves and I think I've seen enough at this point. If you're a diehard Fallout fan like I used to be, you're going to get your questing hours in and it'll be fine enough, I actually do think there's some quests here that approach decent. But with all the hype around the Wastelanders update "fixing" this game, I can't imagine a game that feels more incomplete in its inclusion of people.

See, at its core, Fallout 76 is a game about missing out. You spend the entire game learning about person after person who is no longer here, whole towns wiped out by a magical illness, and there's a distinct sense of loss there and the mourning of a Fallout game that might have taken place a couple years prior to this one. The microtransaction store almost kind of rebuffs this point in regards to FOMO, and as someone who struggles with FOMO in monetized game systems, it feels like a direct extension of the main thing the game seems to be getting at, and I think there's at least something interesting there. That this game encourages that fear of missing out, that this game constantly shows you players who obtained items before you which you could never obtain yourself, is an interesting statement almost as a public experiment to discover the feeling more distinctly. But like Vault-Tec, Bethesda's experiment on the public in FO76 comes off as merely a facade which hides in plain sight something that is, as always, deeply sinister and predatory.

Further, the Wastelanders update betrays this so deeply. It's so odd reading journal entries from... myself, talking about how nobody's in Appalachia anymore, while I'm standing in the Whitespring surrounded by people. I feel like this game probably had a better atmosphere before the Wastelanders update, I'm again regretful that I missed out like this game so deeply wants me to feel. The people they've added never make any sense, sometimes it feels like they were simply obligated to throw random people in random locations that have their one quirk, like Bethesda is saying "here, fine, have your stupid people and your stupid factions and your stupid moral decisions you love oh so much." The two new factions this update added, the Settlers and the Raiders, feel so utterly generic and surface-level that I can't bring myself to care about them at all. Good guy, bad guy. Ooh, which one will you choose? The Overseer is such a corny character I can't get over it, I hate her and her million inexplicable holotapes so much. She wants to break into a Vault full of gold to establish a currency, a regulated capitalist market and a government, and I was shocked to find the dialogue actually lets me disagree with her on the basis of this taking away my freedoms. I did a few times in a row, until she basically said "look, we're going in and doing this whether you want to or not, so shut up and do it". Why would you ever put this option in the dialogue and not let me act on it?? To remind me how little choice I have in this?? What a complete joke, punchline and all.

The joy in this game is in its players, sadly, who I endeavored to avoid as long as possible until some questlines started requiring that I do certain things in public events or teams to progress. You cannot complete many of these side quests without interacting with this multiplayer aspect of the game which I desperately wish didn't exist. The inability to rid yourself of certain items any other way led to multiple high level players stopping me to emote, dropping 500 stimpaks or bullets or something in front of me which awkwardly made me over-encumbered upon picking up (aid and ammo items now weigh things in this game so it's necessary to drop them at a certain point), and then I'd inevitably go do the same thing to some poor schlub who just stumbled out of the Vault for the first time. I really do think the people in this game are kind for that though, and I appreciate those better interactions even if I desperately did not want to have them. Bethesda is cruel to them for treating this still so incomplete game the way they do.

Another highlight is the exploration. This is a rich world to discover and walking the long road through it all, alone and by yourself, really is exciting and fun for the first time. The quests send you back to it and instead force you to mine the game for resources. The Scorchbeasts you feared and who are hard to kill are doomed to repeated slaughter by you later in the game, mindlessly teleporting from fissure to fissure, burning through an endless supply of stimpaks and shotgun shells, waiting for the grind to be over. This is something more typical to the MMORPG genre, and it's why I avoid them like the plague. What a waste of time to beat this beautifully crafted world until it's dead three times over, what a tragic mistake not to instead fill it with deep, intriguing storylines rather than busywork. While this is a wonderful world to discover, it's only skin-deep and its quests seldom meet the splendor of the hills and valleys that feel so much more full of potential when you haven't yet looked behind the curtain. I found Rose and MODUS to be the most interesting parts of this game personally, the former being a somewhat interesting story (despite her annoying voice) and the latter's aesthetic presentation being undeniably inspired.

If you're a Fallout fan in need of some chores, this has chores for you to do and they are in fact Fallout themed. If you're an RPG fan looking for good story, skip it like the plague. If you're a shooter fan looking for things to point guns at, this does a fine job at that. I like the character creation, photo mode, outfit selection, all that... but every game with a good enough system like this will have me returning repeatedly for yet more slop. Do as I say, not as I do, and all that. Avoid this game if you want something worth your time, as always, even if there are nuggets of gold hidden here and there.

Fallout 76 — Um jogo bom prejudicado por uma experiência ruim

Fallout 76 é, sem dúvida, um jogo interessante. O universo é cativante, a narrativa tem potencial e existe muito conteúdo capaz de prender o jogador. Porém, minha experiência particular foi extremamente frustrante por um motivo que considero grave: a navegação e a acessibilidade dos menus são péssimas.

O jogo é excessivamente burocrático.

A construção do CAMP é um dos maiores exemplos. Em praticamente qualquer outro jogo de sobrevivência, construir uma pequena base com quatro ou seis blocos é algo rápido e intuitivo. No Fallout 76, uma tarefa simples pode consumir 10, 15 ou até 20 minutos, não porque a construção seja complexa, mas porque o sistema é contraintuitivo, possui diversos menus e exige uma navegação desnecessariamente complicada.

A localização das peças, a seleção dos objetos e todo o processo de construção parecem ter sido projetados para dificultar algo que deveria ser simples e prazeroso.
.

E o problema não termina aí.

O Pip-Boy e o inventário também são extremamente difíceis de navegar. Quando você acumula muitos itens, encontrar aquilo que realmente precisa pode se tornar uma tarefa cansativa e estressante. Em determinadas situações, existem itens que deveriam ser consumíveis, mas que não podem ser utilizados da maneira esperada, seja por limitações do sistema ou até mesmo por problemas que parecem bugs.

O mesmo problema aparece no acesso às lojas, ao passe de temporada e a outras funções do jogo. Os menus não são facilmente acessíveis e não existe uma navegação realmente fluida entre os diferentes sistemas.

É impressionante que um jogo com tantos recursos tenha uma interface que, em vez de facilitar a vida do jogador, parece constantemente colocar obstáculos no caminho dele.

E isso tem uma consequência muito séria: a desistência acontece antes de o jogador desenvolver uma paixão pelo jogo.

Antes de você ter tempo para se apaixonar pelo universo, descobrir tudo o que Fallout 76 tem a oferecer e criar uma relação com seu personagem e sua base, o jogo já está exigindo paciência para lidar com menus, inventário, construção e navegação.

O jogo deveria estar te divertindo. Em vez disso, ele começa te estressando.

Minha crítica não é contra a proposta de Fallout 76. Pelo contrário: justamente porque o jogo tem potencial, considero ainda mais frustrante ver uma experiência tão interessante sendo prejudicada por sistemas de interface e navegação tão mal resolvidos.

Fallout 76 é um bom jogo com uma péssima experiência de navegação.

Para mim, a avaliação é negativa.

Antes de adicionar ainda mais conteúdo, acredito que Fallout 76 precisaria de uma revisão profunda na interface, nos menus, no inventário, na construção e na acessibilidade geral.

Porque não adianta oferecer um mundo enorme e interessante se o jogador precisa lutar contra o próprio jogo para conseguir utilizá-lo.
